issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette:
Leilani Mahi'ai is an 80-year-old retired welder who has been married to Kimo for 55 years. In the early years of their marriage, Kimo would come home from the bar and strike her with his fists and belt, sometimes pinning her to the floor until she stopped resisting. She never left—she believed it was her wifely duty to endure, and that the beatings were a sign of his passion. Now Kimo is frail and dependent on her, but the old threats are gone. Yet Leilani cannot shake the conviction that her body has been permanently ruined. Her lower back aches constantly from the times he kicked her ribs; her hands tremble when she tries to hold a coffee cup, a tremor she blames equally on decades of welding and on the nights he twisted her arms behind her back. She has come to believe that her body is fundamentally unreliable—a piece of equipment that failed her and can never be repaired.

This belief drives her nightly ritual. She wakes at two in the morning, every single night, her heart hammering, and slides out of bed to check that the front door is bolted and that Kimo is still asleep in his recliner. She listens for his footsteps on the porch, even though he no longer walks anywhere without his walker. She feels on guard inside her own home, scanning the living room shadows as if expecting an attack. The hypervigilance exhausts her, but it also confirms what she already knows: that she is damaged, that her body cannot be trusted even to rest. The more she wakes and checks, the more she becomes certain that she will never feel normal emotions again—that the part of her that once laughed easily or wept freely has been beaten out of her for good.

Because Leilani believes her body is permanently broken, she feels she must remain in a state of constant readiness against further harm—even from a husband who can no longer lift his own cane. This alertness, night after night, then reinforces her appraisals: she interprets her own vigilance as proof that she is indeed too fragile to live without watchfulness, and that her emotions are so blunted she can no longer trust herself to respond to danger appropriately. The cycle has tightened over the decades.

She no longer goes into the basement where Kimo’s old tool bench sits; the smell of grease and rust makes her chest seize, and she avoids the narrow staircase for fear her unsteady legs will give way—a fear that has kept her from using that part of her own home for years. Her children have noticed her distance; she never hugs her grandchildren, because she is certain she cannot feel the warmth they expect. Her daughter finally insisted she see someone after Leilani admitted she had not slept through the night in three decades. What frightens Leilani most is not the memories themselves but the certainty that her body has become a foreign thing she can no longer command—and that she will spend whatever years remain waking alone in the dark, guarding a ghost.
